birr.intro: Birr Castle's oldest tree, the Carroll Oak, was planted before the Parsons family arrived in 1620, and probably around 1550. It stands in the open parkland of the demesne. Near the castle, on the lower terrace of the Formal Gardens, are box hedges the castle calls the tallest in the world, somewhere between nine and twelve metres depending on who measured. A dawn redwood grown from 1940s seed completes the three. All of them are inside the ticketed demesne, open all year.
birr.meta_description: Birr Castle's old trees: the Carroll Oak from before 1620, the world's tallest box hedges by the castle's account, and a 1940s dawn redwood.
birr.question_meta: Birr's oldest tree is the Carroll Oak in Birr Castle Demesne, planted before 1620 and probably around 1550.
birr.question_answer: Birr's oldest mapped tree is the Carroll Oak, a Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) in the parkland of Birr Castle Demesne. The estate says it was planted before the Parsons family arrived in 1620; the Irish Times put its planting around 1550.
birr.question_context: The oak carries the name of the O'Carroll clan, who held Birr until the 1620s, though the estate does not say who planted it. In 2005 the Irish Times reckoned it had been planted about 455 years earlier and was set to last roughly as long again. The national heritage tree register gave it 300 to 500 years in 2009 and recorded it as a maiden oak, a single trunk never cut back. No girth or height has been published. The demesne's box hedges are at least two centuries old, with sources ranging from the 1780s to more than 300 years. The estate says the oak was certainly planted before the Parsons family arrived in 1620, and it is the only tree it places before them. In 2005 a trimmed circle was kept clear around its base. The box hedges stand on the lower terrace of the Formal Gardens, and the castle calls them the tallest in the world, though published heights run from nine to twelve metres. A dawn redwood from seed that reached Birr in the 1940s completes the three trees mapped here. The demesne is ticketed and open all year.

faq.q: How old is the Carroll Oak at Birr?
faq.a: More than four centuries. The estate says it predates 1620, the Irish Times put its planting around 1550, and the register gave 300 to 500 years in 2009.

faq.q: How tall are the Birr Castle box hedges?
faq.a: Somewhere between nine and twelve metres. The castle calls them the tallest in the world but gives no figure, and published heights range from 31 feet to about 40.

faq.q: Can you see the trees for free?
faq.a: No. All three are inside Birr Castle Demesne, which is ticketed and open all year. The castle itself is a private home.

emo.intro: Emo Court's great yew is 4.37 metres round and 14 metres tall, a many-stemmed tree in the parkland south-east of the house. A yew at Emo was measured in 1794 by Samuel Hayes for his Practical Treatise on Trees; whether it was this one, nobody can prove. The national register gives it 200 to 300 years as of 2009, so somewhere between 200 and 400 today. The gardens and parkland are run by the Office of Public Works and open all year in daylight.
emo.meta_description: The Emo Court yew in Co. Laois: 4.37 metres round, many-stemmed, perhaps the yew measured here in 1794. Parkland open all year in daylight.
emo.question_meta: Emo's oldest tree is the many-stemmed yew in the Emo Court parkland, aged somewhere between 200 and 400 years.
emo.question_answer: Emo's oldest mapped tree is the European Yew (Taxus baccata) in the parkland of Emo Court, 4.37 metres round and 14 metres tall in 2009. Its age is estimated at somewhere between 200 and 400 years.
emo.question_context: The Tree Register of Ireland measured the yew in August 2009 and listed it as number 54. The national heritage tree register recorded one yew at Emo on the same day, in coppice form, and gave it 200 to 300 years. Both records very probably describe the same tree, though neither says so. Samuel Hayes measured a yew at Emo in 1794 and included it in his Practical Treatise on Trees. The Ancient Yew Group asks whether this is that tree and leaves the question open. If it is, the yew was already worth measuring more than 230 years ago. In 2009 the yew measured 4.37 metres round and 14 metres tall, which put it in the Tree Register's ancient class. It grows as a coppice, many stems rising from one base. Counting the years since 2009, the register's band comes out at roughly 200 to 300 years or a little more. Emo Court is managed by the Office of Public Works, and Laois County Council says the gardens and parkland are open all year in daylight.

faq.q: How old is the Emo Court yew?
faq.a: Somewhere between 200 and 400 years. The register gave 200 to 300 in 2009; a yew measured here in 1794 may be the same tree.
4.37 metres round and 14 metres tall when the Tree Register of Ireland measured it in 2009, with many stems rising from one base.
Laois County Council says the gardens and parkland are open all year in daylight. The house is a separate guided tour; check heritageireland.ie for seasonal hours.

inistioge.intro: Woodstock, just outside Inistioge, holds a gnarled giant sequoia that the Irish Times called the widest tree in Ireland in 1999, 7.65 metres round at its base and 41.5 metres tall. Woodstock's own page now gives Ireland's largest giant redwood as bigger, so the crown has moved on. In the same arboretum stands what the estate calls its Champion Coast redwood, one of a pair. Both are put at roughly 150 to 215 years. Entry is five euro per car.
inistioge.meta_description: Woodstock Gardens near Inistioge: a gnarled giant sequoia 41.5 metres tall and the estate's champion coast redwood. Five euro per car.
inistioge.question_meta: Inistioge's best-known tree is Woodstock's gnarled giant sequoia, 41.5 metres tall and 7.65 metres round at its base in 1999.
inistioge.question_answer: Inistioge's best-known tree is the giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) in Woodstock Gardens and Arboretum, measured at 41.5 metres tall and 7.65 metres round at its base in 1999. It is roughly 150 to 215 years old.
inistioge.question_context: The Irish Times reported the sequoia during the restoration of Woodstock's Victorian gardens in 1999 and called it the tallest tree in the park and the widest in Ireland. Woodstock's own page now gives Ireland's largest recorded giant redwood as 51 metres tall and 8.6 metres round, so the widest claim no longer stands. The girth was taken at the base, not at chest height. The national heritage tree register put the sequoia at 150 to 200 years in 2009, and the species reached Ireland only in the 1850s. The estate's champion coast redwood is one of two in the arboretum, about 67 metres apart, and nobody has published which. The tree is older looking and twisted, and two stately Wellingtonias stood almost 40 metres tall nearby in 1999. No newer measurement has been published since. Woodstock is run by Kilkenny County Council, entry is five euro per car, and the gardens close whenever a yellow, orange or red weather warning is in force.

faq.q: Is the Woodstock sequoia the widest tree in Ireland?
faq.a: The Irish Times said so in 1999, at 7.65 metres round its base. Woodstock's own page now names a larger giant redwood, so the claim no longer holds.

faq.q: How old are the Woodstock redwoods?
faq.a: Roughly 150 to 215 years. The register gave 150 to 200 in 2009, and the giant sequoia only reached Ireland in the 1850s.
Five euro per car. The gardens open daily and close whenever a yellow, orange or red weather warning is in force.

castlepollard.intro: The Squire's Walking Stick at Tullynally Castle, two kilometres from Castlepollard, is the tallest oak in the Republic of Ireland according to the Irish Times. The Telegraph put it at 112 feet, about 34 metres, and dated its planting to 1745, both from that one article. The national register suggests it is younger, so its age runs from about 200 to 280 years. It stands on the left of the main avenue as you leave, in parkland Tullynally opens to walkers all year.
castlepollard.meta_description: The Squire's Walking Stick at Tullynally, Castlepollard: reported as Ireland's tallest oak, about 34 metres, beside the main avenue.
castlepollard.question_meta: Castlepollard's tallest tree is the Squire's Walking Stick at Tullynally, reported as the tallest oak in the Republic of Ireland.
castlepollard.question_answer: Castlepollard's best-known tree is the Squire's Walking Stick, a Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) beside the main avenue of Tullynally Castle. The Irish Times calls it the tallest oak in the Republic; the Telegraph gave 112 feet, about 34 metres.
castlepollard.question_context: Tullynally's own tree trail names the Walking Stick as the tallest oak in the demesne and places it on the left of the main avenue on the way out. A Telegraph piece on private arboretums called it the tallest oak in Ireland at 112 feet and said the first Baron Longford planted it in 1745; both figures come from that article alone. The national heritage tree register put the demesne's named oak at 150 to 200 years in 2009, about a century younger, and whether that entry is this tree has not been shown. The estate's trail also includes a young oak bred from it. Thomas Pakenham, whose family owns Tullynally, has written about these grounds in In the Company of Trees. The estate says its parkland is open to walkers all year, with dogs on leads, while the gardens are ticketed and open from late March to late September. Which side of that line this stretch of avenue falls on is not stated. No girth for the oak has been published, and no measurement checks the 112 feet.

faq.q: Is the Squire's Walking Stick the tallest oak in Ireland?
faq.a: The Irish Times calls it the tallest in the Republic and the Telegraph the tallest in Ireland, at 112 feet. No independent measurement has been published.
Somewhere between about 200 and 280 years. The Telegraph says planted in 1745; the national register suggests a century younger.
Tullynally says its parkland is open to walkers all year, dogs on leads. The gardens are ticketed and seasonal, so ask at reception which side the avenue falls on.

killarney.intro: The yew at the centre of the cloister of Muckross Friary, about four kilometres from Killarney town, is likely up to 400 years old according to the Office of Public Works, while local tradition says it was planted with the friary around 1448. Its red, twisting trunk measured 305 centimetres round at the ground in 2005, almost exactly what it measured in 1897. In 1756 its crown already spread like an umbrella over the cloister. The friary is an unguided site inside Killarney National Park.
killarney.meta_description: The Muckross Abbey yew near Killarney: a red, twisting yew in the middle of a 15th-century cloister, up to 400 years old or more by tradition.
killarney.question_meta: Killarney's oldest tree is the yew in the cloister of Muckross Friary, likely up to 400 years old, by tradition as old as the friary.
killarney.question_answer: Killarney's oldest mapped tree is the European Yew (Taxus baccata) in the centre of the cloister at Muckross Friary. The Office of Public Works says it is likely up to 400 years old; local tradition makes it as old as the friary, founded around 1448.
killarney.question_context: Heritage Ireland calls the Muckross yew one of the oldest in Ireland and likely up to 400 years old. Tradition holds that it was planted when Donal McCarthy Mor founded the friary for the Observant Franciscans, around 1448, which would make it about 575. A hollow yew cannot be dated by its rings, so neither figure can be settled. Charles Smith described its umbrella-like crown over the cloister in 1756, and Arthur Young mentioned it in 1776. It measured ten feet round at the ground in 1897 and 305 centimetres in 2005. It is a male tree. A second old yew grows outside the ruin, near the entrance. The friary stands inside Killarney National Park and is cared for by the Office of Public Works. The yew grows from the exact centre of the cloister, its bark red and its trunk twisting as it rises. The friary has lost its roof, and the crown still fills the open square from wall to wall.

faq.q: How old is the Muckross Abbey yew?
faq.a: The Office of Public Works says likely up to 400 years. Tradition says it was planted with the friary around 1448. Neither can be proved from a hollow trunk.
In the exact centre of the cloister of Muckross Friary, inside Killarney National Park, about four kilometres south-east of Killarney town.

faq.q: Does it cost anything to see?
faq.a: Muckross Friary is an unguided Heritage Ireland site. Its page shows no admission charge or opening hours; check it before you go.

gort.intro: The Autograph Tree at Coole Park, about four kilometres from Gort, is a copper beech carved with the initials of W. B. Yeats, John Millington Synge, George Bernard Shaw, Sean O'Casey and others. Yeats cut the first, in 1898, at Lady Gregory's request. The bark is slowly healing over the letters, and a plaque at the base helps read them. It stands just beyond the red gates of the walled garden, in a nature reserve that is free to walk.
gort.meta_description: The Autograph Tree at Coole Park near Gort: a copper beech carved with the initials of Yeats, Synge, Shaw and O'Casey. Free to visit.
gort.question_meta: Gort's most famous tree is the Autograph Tree at Coole Park, a copper beech carved with the initials of Yeats, Synge and Shaw.
gort.question_answer: Gort's most famous tree is the Autograph Tree, a Copper Beech (Fagus sylvatica f. purpurea) in the walled garden of Coole Park. W. B. Yeats carved his initials into it in 1898 at Lady Gregory's request, and Synge, Shaw and O'Casey followed.
gort.question_context: Coole Park says the beech was already mature when Yeats carved his initials in 1898. The names also include Edward Martyn, the painter Jack B. Yeats, the sculptor Theodore Spicer-Simson, the illustrator Elinor Monsell, the Countess of Cromartie and Lady Gregory. Some initials are fading as the bark heals, and a plaque at the base identifies them. The national heritage tree register put the tree at 150 to 200 years in 2009; the 160 and 200 year figures on popular pages give no source. Coole Park is run by the National Parks and Wildlife Service, with free parking at the visitor centre. Lady Gregory asked Yeats to cut his initials in 1898, and John Millington Synge, George Bernard Shaw and Sean O'Casey added theirs. The beech stands just beyond the red gates of the walled garden, where a row of upright Irish yews shelters the hothouses. No girth or height has been published. The park's grounds are open daily, with longer hours in summer.

faq.q: Whose initials are on the Autograph Tree?
faq.a: W. B. Yeats, John Millington Synge, George Bernard Shaw, Sean O'Casey, Edward Martyn, Jack B. Yeats, Lady Gregory and several of her other guests.

faq.q: How old is the Autograph Tree?
faq.a: The national register gave 150 to 200 years in 2009. It was already mature when Yeats carved the first initials in 1898.
Yes. The grounds are open daily, longer hours in summer, with free parking at the visitor centre.
